title: Bekhorot 36
description: Whom to believe about a firstborn’s blemish: hearsay testimony, Rabbi Ile’a’s priest who says “it is a firstborn and its blemish is with it”, the clash between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua over Rabbi Tzadok’s firstborn, the priest who says an Israelite gave it to him blemished, and when three synagogue-goers may permit a firstborn.
topics: 🗣️ Hearsay testimony about a firstborn: Rav Asi and Rav Ashi, and “Yeimar who permits firstborns”
👄 Rabbi Ile’a: “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”, and the rented donkey on the road of Nehar Pekod
🛡️ Rabbi Tzadok’s firstborn splits its lip, and Rabbi Yehoshua is left standing in the study hall
🔍 “Any matter likely to be revealed, people do not lie about it”: the priest, the Israelite and the agent buying tithed produce
👁️ Rafram forces his eyes open and recognizes his own firstborn
🎓 Rav Ashi and the animal with one large eye: brought out of respect for the Sage
🐑 Why everyone is believed about the blemishes of animal tithe
3️⃣ Three synagogue-goers may permit a firstborn: outside the Land, clear-cut blemishes, where there is no expert

a1.he: אֵימַר דְּאָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר לַחֲשָׁשָׁא, לְאַחְזוֹקִינְהוּ מִי אָמַר?

a2.he: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: עֵד מִפִּי עֵד, מַהוּ לְעֵדוּת בְּכוֹר? רַב אַסִּי אָסַר, וְרַב אָשֵׁי שָׁרֵי. אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַסִּי לְרַב אָשֵׁי: וְהָא תָּנָא דְבֵי מְנַשֶּׁה: אֵין עֵד מִפִּי עֵד כָּשֵׁר אֶלָּא לְעֵדוּת הָאִשָּׁה!

a3.he: תְּנִי: אֶלָּא לְעֵדוּת שֶׁהָאִשָּׁה כְּשֵׁרָה לָהּ בִּלְבָד.

a4.he: רַב יֵימַר אַכְשַׁר עֵד מִפִּי עֵד בִּבְכוֹר, קָרֵי עֲלֵיהּ מָרִימָר: ״יֵימַר שָׁרֵי בּוּכְרָא״. וְהִלְכְתָא: עֵד מִפִּי עֵד כָּשֵׁר לְעֵדוּת בְּכוֹר.

a5.he: אָמַר רַבִּי אִילְעָא: לֹא הָיוּ מוּחְזָקִין בּוֹ שֶׁהוּא בְּכוֹר, וּבָא אֶחָד וְאָמַר שֶׁהוּא בְּכוֹר וּמוּמוֹ עִמּוֹ — נֶאֱמָן.

a6.he: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן, שֶׁהַפֶּה שֶׁאָסַר הוּא הַפֶּה שֶׁהִתִּיר? תְּנֵינָא: הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁאָמְרָה ״אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ הָיִיתִי וּגְרוּשָׁה אֲנִי״ נֶאֱמֶנֶת, שֶׁהַפֶּה שֶׁאָסַר הוּא הַפֶּה שֶׁהִתִּיר!

a7.he: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: הָתָם הוּא דְּאִי בָּעֲיָא לָא אָמְרָה. אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּלָא סַגִּיא דְּלָא אָמְרָה, דְּקָדָשִׁים בְּחוּץ לָא אָכֵיל,

a8.he: אֵימָא: לָא הַפֶּה שֶׁאָסַר הוּא, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן, דְּאִי מִשּׁוּם הָכִי — הֲוָה שָׁדֵי בֵּיהּ מוּמָא דְּנִיכָּר וְאָכֵיל לֵיהּ.

a9.he: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי: מַאי שְׁנָא מֵהָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאוֹגַר לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ, וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא תֵּיזִיל בְּאוֹרְחָא דִּנְהַר פְּקוֹד דְּאִיכָּא מַיָּא, זִיל בְּאוֹרְחָא דְּנַרֶשׁ דְּלֵיכָּא מַיָּא. אֲזַל בְּאוֹרְחָא דִּנְהַר פְּקוֹד וּמִית חֲמָרָא, וַאֲתָא וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּאוֹרְחָא דִּנְהַר פְּקוֹד אָזְלִי, וּמִיהוּ מַיָּא לָא הֲווֹ.

a10.he: וַאֲמַר רָבָא: מָה לוֹ לְשַׁקֵּר, אִי בָּעֵי אָמַר: בְּאוֹרְחָא דְּנַרֶשׁ אֲזַלִי. וַאֲמַר אַבָּיֵי: ״מָה לוֹ לְשַׁקֵּר״ בִּמְקוֹם עֵדִים לָא אָמְרִינַן.

a11.he: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא?! הָתָם וַדַּאי אִיכָּא מַיָּא, הָכָא וַדַּאי שָׁדֵי בֵּיהּ מוּמָא — חֲשָׁשָׁא הוּא, וּבִמְקוֹם חֲשָׁשָׁא אָמְרִינַן ״מָה לוֹ לְשַׁקֵּר״. יָתֵיב רָבִינָא וְקָאָמַר לְהַאי שְׁמַעְתָּא בְּלָא גַּבְרָא, אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא זוּטֵי לְרָבִינָא: אֲנַן מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אִילְעָא מַתְנִינַן לַהּ.

a12.he: רַבִּי צָדוֹק הֲוָה לֵיהּ בּוּכְרָא, רְמָא לֵיהּ שְׂעָרֵי בְּסַלֵּי, בַּהֲדֵי דְּקָאָכֵיל אִיבְּזַע שִׂיפְתֵּיהּ. אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, אָמַר לוֹ: כְּלוּם חִילַּקְנוּ בֵּין חָבֵר לְעַם הָאָרֶץ? אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: הֵן.

a13.he: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, אָמַר לוֹ: חִילַּקְנוּ בֵּין חָבֵר לְעַם הָאָרֶץ? אָמַר לוֹ רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: לָא. אָמַר לוֹ: (והא) [וַהֲלֹא] רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אָמַר לִי הֵן! אָמַר לוֹ: הַמְתֵּן עַד שֶׁיַּעֲלוּ בַּעֲלֵי תְרִיסִין לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ.

a14.he: כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּכְנְסוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, עָמַד הַשּׁוֹאֵל וְשָׁאַל: כְּלוּם חִילַּקְנוּ בֵּין חָבֵר לְעַם הָאָרֶץ? אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: לָאו. אָמַר לוֹ רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: וַהֲלֹא מִשִּׁמְךָ אָמְרוּ לִי הֵן!

a15.he: יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, עֲמוֹד עַל רַגְלֶיךָ, וְיָעִידוּ בְּךָ. עָמַד רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ עַל רַגְלָיו וְאָמַר: הֵיאַךְ אֶעֱשֶׂה? אִילְמָלֵי אֲנִי חַי וְהוּא מֵת — יָכוֹל הַחַי לְהַכְחִישׁ אֶת הַמֵּת, עַכְשָׁיו שֶׁאֲנִי חַי וְהוּא חַי — הֵיאַךְ חַי יָכוֹל לְהַכְחִישׁ אֶת הַחַי?

a16.he: וְהָיָה רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל עוֹמֵד וְדוֹרֵשׁ, וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ עוֹמֵד עַל רַגְלָיו, עַד שֶׁרִינְּנוּ כׇּל הָעָם וְאָמְרוּ לְחוּצְפִּית הַמְתוּרְגְּמָן: עֲמוֹד! וְעָמַד.

a17.he: מַתְנִי׳ נֶאֱמָן הַכֹּהֵן לוֹמַר: הֶרְאֵיתִי בְּכוֹר זֶה וּבַעַל מוּם הוּא.

a18.he: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: נֶאֱמָן הַכֹּהֵן לוֹמַר ״בְּכוֹר זֶה נָתַן לִי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּמוּמוֹ״. מַאי טַעְמָא? כֹּל מִילְּתָא דַּעֲבִידָא לְאִיגַּלּוֹיֵי לָא מְשַׁקְּרִי בַּהּ אִינָשֵׁי. אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אַף אֲנַן נָמֵי תְּנֵינָא, נֶאֱמָן הַכֹּהֵן לוֹמַר ״הֶרְאֵיתִי בְּכוֹר זֶה וּבַעַל מוּם הוּא״. מַאי טַעְמָא? לָאו מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמְרִינַן כֹּל מִילְּתָא דַּעֲבִידָא לְאִיגַּלּוֹיֵי לָא מְשַׁקְּרִי בַּהּ אִינָשֵׁי?

a19.he: הָתָם הוּא דְּקָדָשִׁים בְּחוּץ לָא אָכֵיל, אֲבָל הָכָא, כֵּיוָן דַּחֲשִׁידִי — חֲשִׁידִי.

a20.he: מֵתִיב רַב שֵׁיזְבִי: הָאוֹמֵר לְמִי שֶׁאֵין נֶאֱמָן עַל הַמַּעֲשֵׂר ״קַח לִי מִמִּי שֶׁהוּא נֶאֱמָן״ אוֹ ״מִמִּי שֶׁהוּא מְעַשֵּׂר״ — אֵינוֹ נֶאֱמָן. אַמַּאי? נֵימָא: כֹּל מִילְּתָא דַּעֲבִידָא לְאִיגַּלּוֹיֵי לָא מְשַׁקְּרִי בַּהּ אִינָשֵׁי!

b2.he: סֵיפָא וַדַּאי מְסַיְּיעָא לֵיהּ: מֵאִישׁ פְּלוֹנִי — הֲרֵי זֶה נֶאֱמָן.

b3.he: הָתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּאִית לֵיהּ תּוֹבֵעַ, מִירְתַת.

b4.he: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא: מְנָא לֵיהּ לִיהוּדָה הָא? אֲנָא בְּגִידּוּל קְבַעְתָּיהּ, וְגִידּוּל קְבַע בְּדִידֵיהּ. וְהָכִי אָמְרִי לֵיהּ: נֶאֱמָן יִשְׂרָאֵל לוֹמַר ״בְּכוֹר זֶה נָתַתִּי לְכֹהֵן בְּמוּמוֹ״.

b5.he: יִשְׂרָאֵל? פְּשִׁיטָא! לָא צְרִיכָא בְּקָטָן וְהִגְדִּיל, מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: לָא קִים לֵיהּ? קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

b6.he: בְּסוּרָא מַתְנוּ כְּלִשָּׁנָא בָתְרָא, בְּפוּמְבְּדִיתָא כְּלִשָּׁנָא קַמָּא, וְהִלְכְתָא אֲפִילּוּ כְּלִשָּׁנָא קַמָּא.

b7.he: רַפְרָם בְּפוּמְבְּדִיתָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ בּוּכְרָא, וְיַהֲבֵיהּ לֵיהּ לְכֹהֵן בְּלָא מוּמָא. אֲזַל שְׁדָא בֵּיהּ מוּמָא. יוֹמָא חַד חֲלַשׁ בְּעֵינֵיהּ, אַיְיתְיֵהּ לְקַמֵּיהּ. אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּכוֹר זֶה נָתַן לִי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּמוּמוֹ. אַרְפְּסִינֵיהּ לְעֵינֵיהּ, חַזְיֵיהּ בְּשִׁקְרֵיהּ. אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָאו אֲנָא דִּיהֵיבְתֵּיהּ לָךְ?

b8.he: וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי לָא חַשׁ לַהּ לְמִילְּתָא, הַאי הוּא דַּחֲצִיף, כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא חֲצִיפִי.

b9.he: הָהוּא שָׂרוּעַ דַּאֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב אָשֵׁי, אָמַר: לְמַאי נֵיחוּשׁ לֵיהּ? אִי כֹּהֵן הוּא, אִי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא — הֲרֵי בְּכוֹר וּמוּמוֹ עִמּוֹ.

b10.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: וְדִלְמָא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא, וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: אֵין רוֹאִין בְּכוֹר יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן כֹּהֵן עִמּוֹ!

b11.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא?! הָתָם, נְהִי דְּקָדָשִׁים בְּחוּץ לָא אָכֵיל, אַמָּמוֹנֵיהּ דְּכֹהֵן חֲשִׁיד.

b12.he: הָכָא, מִכְּדֵי יָדַע דְּהַאי מוּם מוּבְהָק הוּא, מַאי טַעְמָא אַתְיוּהּ קַמֵּיהּ רַבָּנַן? מִשּׁוּם כְּבוֹדוֹ דְּחָכָם; עַל כְּבוֹדוֹ דְּחָכָם לָא עָבֵיד, אִיסּוּרָא עָבֵד?!

b14.he: גְּמָ׳ מַאי טַעְמָא? דְּאִי בָּעֵי שָׁדֵי בֵּיהּ מוּמָא מֵעִיקָּרָא! מִי יָדַע הֵי נָפֵיק?

b15.he: וְכִי תֵּימָא מַפֵּיק לֵיהּ בְּרֵישׁ עַשְׂרָה, ״לֹא יְבַקֵּר בֵּין טוֹב לָרַע״ אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא! אֶלָּא דְּאִי בָּעֵי שָׁדֵי בֵּיהּ מוּמָא (בכולי) [בְּכוּלֵּיהּ] עֶדְרֵיהּ.

b16.he: מַתְנִי׳ בְּכוֹר שֶׁנִּסְמֵית עֵינוֹ, וְשֶׁנִּקְטְעָה יָדוֹ, וְשֶׁנִּשְׁבְּרָה רַגְלוֹ — הֲרֵי זֶה יִשָּׁחֵט עַל פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי הַכְּנֶסֶת. רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ יֵשׁ שָׁם עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה, אֵינוֹ נִשְׁחָט אֶלָּא עַל פִּי מוּמְחֶה.

b17.he: גְּמָ׳ רַבִּי שִׂמְלַאי וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה תַּרְוַיְיהוּ מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי אָמְרִי, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ: רַבִּי שִׂמְלַאי וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה אָמְרִי: הַתָּרַת בְּכוֹר בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ עַל פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי הַכְּנֶסֶת. אָמַר רָבָא: וּבְמוּמִין מוּבְהָקִין.

b18.he: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? תְּנֵינָא: בְּכוֹר שֶׁנִּסְמֵית עֵינוֹ, וְשֶׁנִּקְטְעָה יָדוֹ, וְשֶׁנִּשְׁתַּבְּרָה רַגְלוֹ — הֲרֵי זֶה יִשָּׁחֵט עַל פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי הַכְּנֶסֶת!

b19.he: אִי מִמַּתְנִיתִין הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: בְּחוּצָה לָאָרֶץ אֲפִילּוּ מוּמִין שֶׁאֵין מוּבְהָקִין, וְהַאי דְּקָתָנֵי מוּבְהָקִין — לְהוֹדִיעֲךָ כֹּחוֹ דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

b20.he: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא, סָפֵק מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב, סָפֵק מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל: שְׁלֹשָׁה מַתִּירִין אֶת הַבְּכוֹר בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מוּמְחֶה. מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? תְּנֵינָא: הֲרֵי זֶה יִשָּׁחֵט עַל פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי הַכְּנֶסֶת!

b21.he: אִי מִמַּתְנִיתִין הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: בִּמְקוֹם מוּמְחֶה, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן: בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מוּמְחֶה — אִין, בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ מוּמְחֶה — לָא.

b22.he: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר עַמְרָם: שְׁלֹשָׁה מַתִּירִין אֶת הַבְּכוֹר בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מוּמְחֶה, שְׁלֹשָׁה מַתִּירִין אֶת הַנֶּדֶר בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין חָכָם. שְׁלֹשָׁה מַתִּירִין אֶת הַבְּכוֹר בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין מוּמְחֶה

messages.text: Continued from 35b: Rav Pappa asked Abaye: according to Rabbi Meir, one suspect about a matter may neither judge nor testify about it, and one suspected of one matter is suspected of the entire Torah. If so, priests should not judge at all; yet it is written of them: “And according to their word shall every controversy and every stroke be.”

One can say that Rabbi Meir says that priests are suspect with regard to causing blemishes only to the extent that there is a concern that they might have caused a blemish. But did he say this ruling to establish them as those who definitely cause blemishes? Certainly not.

notes.he: בחשודים מי אמר ר"מ חשוד לדבר אחד חשוד לכל התורה כולה היכא דמוחזק לן דעובר על דבר א':
notes.en: To establish them: as suspects. Did Rabbi Meir say “one suspected of one matter is suspected of the entire Torah” [about them]? [He said it only] where it is established for us that a person transgresses one matter.

notes.he: מתוך הלשון משמע דאליבא דר' מאיר קאמר ולא סבירא לן כוותיה אלא אפילו במוחזק עובר על דבר א' לא הוי חשוד על כל התורה כולה ואע"ג דבפרק זה בורר (סנהדרין דף כז.) אמר אביי עבריין אוכל נבילות להכעיס פסול לעדות ומוקים לה כרבי מאיר וקיימא לן כוותיה דהוא מיע"ל קג"ם היינו דוקא לענין עדות דרחמנא אמר אל תשת רשע עד אבל בשאר מילי לא חשיד ומיהו ר' מאיר דקאמר התם עד זומם פסול לכל התורה כולה ה"נ הוה מצי למינקט אחד משאר דברים ולא נקט עד זומם אלא לאפוקי מדר' יוסי דאפילו עד זומם נמי מכשר לדיני נפשות כשהוזם בדיני ממונות:
notes.en: Granted that Rabbi Meir said this with regard to a concern, etc.: From the wording it appears that this is said according to Rabbi Meir, and we do not hold like him; rather, even one established as transgressing one matter is not suspected regarding the entire Torah. And although in the chapter Zeh Borer (Sanhedrin 27a) Abaye said that a transgressor who eats carcasses provocatively is disqualified from testimony, and it is established according to Rabbi Meir, and we hold like him, since it is one of [the six rulings where the halakha follows Abaye, mnemonic] Ya’al Kagam, that is specifically with regard to testimony, for the Merciful One said: “Do not put your hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness”; but in other matters he is not suspected. However, Rabbi Meir, who says there that a conspiring witness is disqualified for the entire Torah, could equally have mentioned any of the other matters; he mentioned a conspiring witness only to exclude the view of Rabbi Yosei, who validates even a conspiring witness for capital cases when he was found conspiring in monetary cases.

notes.he: אימור דאמר ר' מאיר החשוד על הדבר לחששא בעלמא בשמא חשיד לא חזוקינהו נמי דודאי חשידי לא אמרינן הלכך לא חשידי לכל התורה וכשירין למידן:
notes.en: Granted that Rabbi Meir said “one suspected about a matter” with regard to a mere concern, where perhaps he is suspected; to establish them as certainly suspected he did not say [it]. Therefore they are not suspected regarding the entire Torah, and they are fit to judge.

messages.text: A dilemma was raised before the Sages: With regard to testimony based on hearsay, where one repeats the testimony of another witness, what is the halakha in a case of such testimony about a blemished firstborn animal?

notes.he: להעיד שלא הטיל בו מום זה בכוונה:
notes.en: For testimony about a firstborn: to testify that he did not inflict this blemish deliberately.

messages.text: Rav Asi deems prohibited the slaughter of the animal based on such testimony, and Rav Ashi deems it permitted.

But isn’t it taught in a baraita in the school of Menashe that hearsay testimony is valid only for the testimony of a woman, where one testifies that her husband is dead? This indicates that such testimony is not accepted in all other instances.
Emend the baraita and teach it like this: Testimony based on hearsay is valid only for that testimony for which the testimony of a woman is valid.
messages.quote: hearsay testimony is valid only for the testimony of a woman

notes.he: שמת בעלה במדינת הים:
notes.en: For the testimony of a woman: [testimony] that her husband died overseas.

notes.he: ובעדות בכור נמי אשה כשרה דאמרינן הלכתא כרבן שמעון ואפי' בתו:
notes.en: Teach: only for testimony for which a woman is valid: and in testimony about a firstborn a woman is also valid, since we say that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon [ben Gamliel], and even his daughter [may testify].

notes.he: ואשה כשרה לעדות בכור מדאמרי' אפילו בנו אפי' בתו:
notes.en: For testimony for which a woman is valid. And a woman is valid for testimony about a firstborn, since we say: even his son, even his daughter.

messages.text: According to Rav Ashi, the baraita is teaching that any case where the testimony of a woman is valid, hearsay testimony is valid as well, and this includes testimony concerning a blemished firstborn animal.
Rav Yeimar deemed fit testimony based on hearsay with regard to a blemished firstborn animal.
Yeimar who permits firstborn animals.

notes.he: יימר המתיר בכורות לשון גנאי:
notes.en: Yeimar permits firstborns: “Yeimar, the one who permits firstborns”, a derogatory expression.

messages.text: And the halakha is that testimony based on hearsay is valid in the case of a firstborn animal.

In a case where a blemished animal was not established as being a firstborn, and one priest came to an expert and said that it is a firstborn animal and yet its blemish is with it, i.e., it was unintentionally blemished, he is deemed credible, and the expert may deem the animal fit for slaughter based on the priest’s testimony.

notes.he: בטלה שהוא בכור ובא כהן בעליו ואמר בכור הוא זה ומומו עמו שלא הוטל מום זה בכוונה ואתי לאחוויי לחכם אי קבוע הוא אי עובר הוא:
notes.en: They were not established: that it is a firstborn, and the priest, its owner, came and said: This is a firstborn and its blemish is with it, meaning this blemish was not inflicted deliberately; and he came to show it to a Sage [to find out] whether it is permanent or passing.

notes.he: דהפה שאסר ואמר בכור הוא התיר ואמר מומו עמו:
notes.en: He is deemed credible: for the mouth that prohibited, by saying “it is a firstborn”, is the mouth that permitted, by saying “its blemish is with it”.

messages.text: What is Rabbi Ile’a teaching us? Is he teaching us the principle that the mouth that prohibited it is the mouth that permitted it, i.e., when the only source that an item was prohibited is the statement of one who says that it is now permitted, his claim is accepted? But we learn this in a mishna:

With regard to a woman who said: I was a married woman and now I am a divorcée, she is deemed credible and permitted to remarry, as the mouth that prohibited her by establishing that she was married is the mouth that permitted her by establishing that she was divorced.

notes.he: ולא היינו מוחזקין בה שהיא אשת איש מעולם:
notes.en: I was a married woman: and we had never established that she was a married woman.

notes.he: ומותרת להנשא:
notes.en: She is deemed credible: and she is permitted to marry.

messages.text: Rabbi Ile’a’s statement is necessary, lest you say it is only there, in the case of the mishna, that the woman’s testimony is accepted, as, if she wants to remarry illegally, she does not need to say anything at all about previously being married.

notes.he: כלומר אי הוה חשידא להינשא בחיי בעלה בלא גירושין הוה שתקה ולא אמרה אשת איש הייתי דהא בפנויה מחזקינן לה:
notes.en: For if she wanted she would not have said it: that is, if she were suspected of marrying during her husband’s lifetime without a divorce, she would have kept silent and not said “I was a married woman”, for we presume her to be unmarried.

notes.he: גבי אשה דאמרינן הפה שאסר הוא שהתיר דאי בעיא לא אמרה מידי ולא מחזקינן לה באשת איש דליכא דידע:
notes.en: Lest you say it is there: with a woman we say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”, for if she wanted she would say nothing, and we would not presume her to be a married woman, as no one knows.

messages.text: But here, with regard to the firstborn animal, it is different, as, if the priest wishes to eat the meat of the animal, it not sufficient for him not to bring the animal to an expert, i.e., he has no recourse other than to say that it is a firstborn animal which has a blemish requiring examination, as he cannot determine on his own whether this blemish permanently disqualifies the firstborn animal from sacrifice, and he would not eat sacrificial meat outside the Temple courtyard, which is punishable by karet.

notes.he: בבכור דלא סגיא דלא אמר בכור הוא דלימא ליה חכם מום קבוע הוא או עובר דקדשים תמימים אין הכהן נחשד לאכול בחוץ דבר כרת הוא אבל נחשד להטיל בו מום דלאו בעלמא הוא ולא יהא נאמן קמ"ל דנאמן:
notes.en: But here: with a firstborn, where he cannot avoid saying “it is a firstborn”, so that the Sage will tell him whether it is a permanent or a passing blemish. For with unblemished consecrated animals the priest is not suspected of eating them outside [the Temple], as that is a matter of karet; but he is suspected of inflicting a blemish on it, which is a mere prohibition. So [one might think] he should not be credible. [Rabbi Ile’a] teaches us that he is credible.

messages.text: Since the priest must admit that this is a firstborn animal, I might say that this is not a case of: The mouth that prohibited it is the mouth that permitted it, and therefore the priest is not deemed credible.

To dispel this possibility, Rabbi Ile’a teaches us that he is deemed credible, because if it is due to that reason, that the priest is suspected of causing the blemish, he would have caused a blemish that is obvious to all, and then eaten it. In such a case, he would violate a mere prohibition, not one that is punishable by karet, since he would not be eating sacrificial meat outside the Temple courtyard, as the animal is blemished.

notes.he: דהוא הטיל בו מום הוה שדי ביה מום הניכר אפי' לעם הארץ שהוא מום ותו לא הוה בעי למיתי קמן ולמימר בכור הוא דהא אין אדם אחר יודע שהוא בכור ובקדשים בחוץ נמי ליכא לספוקיה דהא מום ניכר שדא ביה והיכא דאנן יודעין שהוא בכור ליכא למימר הכי דבעל כרחך אתי לקמן דאי הוה שחיט ליה בלא מומחה כיון דכולי עלמא ידעי שהוא בכור הוו חשדי ליה:
notes.en: For if so: if he had inflicted a blemish on it, he would have inflicted a blemish recognizable as a blemish even to an ignoramus, and he would no longer need to come before us and say “it is a firstborn”, for no one else knows that it is a firstborn; and as for consecrated meat outside [the Temple], he would have no doubt either, since he inflicted an obvious blemish on it. But where we know that it is a firstborn, one cannot say this, for he is forced to come before us: if he slaughtered it without an expert, since everyone knows that it is a firstborn, they would suspect him.

notes.he: גבי בכור לא סגי דלא אמרה דלא מסהיד דכיון דידע דבכור הוא דקדשים בחוץ נמי לא אכיל אלא א"כ יעיד עליו שהוא מום לא נימא הפה שאסר הוא שהתיר קמ"ל דאמרינן דכיון דיכול למישדי ביה מומא דמינכר ודאי דמום קבוע ולא שדא אמרינן הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר:
notes.en: But here: with a firstborn, he cannot avoid saying [it is a firstborn] and having [the expert] testify, since he knows that it is a firstborn, and he will not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple] unless [the expert] testifies about it that it is a blemish; so let us not say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”. [Rabbi Ile’a] teaches us that we do say it: since he could have inflicted on it an obvious blemish, which is certainly permanent, and he did not, we say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”.

messages.text: What is different between this case and that incident involving a certain man who rented a donkey to another? The owner said to the renter: Look, do not go on the path of Nehar Pekod, where there is water and the donkey is likely to drown. Instead, go on the path of Neresh, where there is no water.
messages.lead: Mar bar Rav Ashi objects to this:
messages.quote: he would have caused a blemish that is obvious to all

messages.text: The renter went on the path of Nehar Pekod and the donkey died. When he came back, he said: Yes, I went on the path of Nehar Pekod, but there was no water there, and therefore the donkey’s death was caused by other factors.

The renter’s claim is accepted, due to the reasoning of: Why would he lie and state this claim? In other words, if this man wanted to lie, he could have told the donkey’s owner: I went on the path of Neresh, as the owner instructed.

notes.he: רבה גרסינן שהיה רבו של אביי ולא רבא דרבא אית ליה בהדיא בחזקת הבתים (ב"ב דף לג:) דמה לו לשקר במקום עדים לא אמרינן דאמר דאביי ורבא לא סבירא להו הא דרב חסדא כו':
notes.en: And Rava said: why would he lie: We read “Rabba”, who was Abaye’s teacher, and not “Rava”. For Rava explicitly holds in [the chapter] Ḥezkat HaBatim (Bava Batra 33b) that we do not say “why would he lie” where there are witnesses, since it says there that Abaye and Rava do not accept that [ruling] of Rav Ḥisda, etc.

messages.text: @Rava We do not say the principle of: Why would he lie, in a place where there are witnesses. Since witnesses can be summoned to establish conclusively whether there was water along the path of Nehar Pekod, the reasoning that the renter could have stated a different claim is not employed.

notes.he: דאנן סהדי דכל שעתא איכא מיא וה"נ כיון דאנן סהדי דכהנים חשודים על המומין לא נימא מה לי לשקר:
notes.en: In a place of witnesses: for we are witnesses that there is water there at all times. So too here, since we are witnesses that priests are suspected about blemishes, let us not say “why would he lie”.

messages.text: Similarly, the priest’s contention that the blemish occurred inadvertently should not be deemed credible, as it is known that priests are suspected of causing blemishes.

How can these cases be compared? There, with regard to the path of Nehar Pekod, there is certainly water there, but here, the possibility that the priest caused a blemish in the firstborn animal is only a concern, and in a place of mere concern we do say the reasoning of: Why would he lie?
messages.quote: it is known that priests are suspected of causing blemishes

notes.he: בתמיה:
notes.en: Here, did he certainly inflict a blemish on it? Said in astonishment.

notes.dh: מה לי לשקר במקום עדים לא אמרינן
notes.he: דאנן סהדי דאורחא דנהר פקוד לעולם איכא מיא והכא נמי כיון דידעינן דכהני חשידי אמומי לא נימא הפה שאסר הוא שהתיר: הכא גבי האי כהן דבא ואמר בכור הוא ומומו עמו מי ידעינן ודאי דאיהו שדא ביה מומא חששא בעלמא הוא ובמקום חששא אמרינן הפה שאסר הוא שהתיר:
notes.en: We do not say “why would he lie” in a place of witnesses: for we are witnesses that on the road of Nehar Pekod there is always water. So too here, since we know that priests are suspected about blemishes, let us not say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”. Here, with this priest who came and said “it is a firstborn and its blemish is with it”, do we know for certain that he inflicted a blemish on it? It is a mere concern, and in a place of concern we say “the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted”.

messages.text: Ravina was sitting and saying this halakha of Rabbi Ile’a anonymously.

notes.he: דר' אילעאי:
notes.en: This teaching: of Rabbi Ile’a.

notes.he: בסתמא אמר ליה לא היו מוחזקין בו שהוא בכור כו':
notes.en: Without [naming] the man: he stated it anonymously: “If they had not established that it is a firstborn,” etc.

messages.text: @Ravina We learned this halakha in the name of Rabbi Ile’a.
Rabbi Tzadok, an erudite priest, had a firstborn animal. He placed barley in wicker baskets for it, and while it was eating, its lip split, rendering the animal blemished.

notes.he: נצרין של ערבה קלופה שהן דקין וחדין:
notes.en: Wicker baskets [natzrin hutzin]: baskets of peeled willow, which are thin and sharp. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s wording; our text of the Gemara has simply “baskets”.]

messages.text: Rabbi Tzadok came before Rabbi Yehoshua, to ask whether or not he is suspected of intentionally causing a blemish in his firstborn animal offering.
@Rabbi Yehoshua Didn’t we differentiate between a priest who is a ḥaver, i.e., learned, and a priest who is an ignoramus, with regard to their credibility about blemishes found on a firstborn animal?

notes.dh: כלום חילקנו בין כהן חבר לכהן עם הארץ
notes.he: ומי חשדינן אנא למישדי ביה מומא בכוונה ככהן עם הארץ:
notes.en: Did we differentiate between a priest who is a ḥaver and a priest who is an ignoramus: and am I suspected of deliberately inflicting a blemish on it, like an ignorant priest?

notes.he: דאע"ג דע"ה חשיד למיגרם מום לבכור כדאמר בעליו עמנו מעידין אי לא לא [כהן] חבר לא חשיד ושלא מדעתו היה מצינא לאסהודי עליה אי לא א"ל ר' יהושע הין:
notes.en: Did we differentiate between a ḥaver and an ignoramus: that although an ignoramus is suspected of causing a blemish in a firstborn, as it says, “if its owners are with us they may testify, and if not, not,” a priest who is a ḥaver is not suspected, and [since the blemish happened] without his intent, I could testify about it; or not? Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: Yes.

messages.text: Yes, we did. Since you are a learned priest, you are deemed credible to testify that this blemish was caused inadvertently.

notes.he: חלקנו ולא חשידת:
notes.en: Yes: we differentiated, and you are not suspected.

messages.text: Rabbi Tzadok then came before Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi and head of the academy of Yavne at the time.
@Rabban Gamliel Didn’t we differentiate between a priest who is a ḥaver and a priest who is an ignoramus with regard to credibility about blemishes found on a firstborn animal?
No, we did not.

notes.dh: בא לפני רבן גמליאל אמר ליה לאו
notes.he: והלכה כן הוא דאין חילוק בין חבר לעם הארץ דבפרק בתרא דיומא (דף עח.) גבי ר' יוסי בן זימרא דכהן הוה ומיבעיא ליה אי הלכה כר' מאיר דאמר חשוד על הדבר לא דנו ולא מעידו אי כרשב"ג דאמר נאמן על של חבירו ש"מ דלרבי מאיר לא היה מתיר אע"פ שהיה חבר:
notes.en: He came before Rabban Gamliel; he said to him: No: And this is the halakha, that there is no distinction between a ḥaver and an ignoramus. For in the last chapter of Yoma (78a), regarding Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, who was a priest, it was asked whether the halakha follows Rabbi Meir, who says one suspected about a matter may neither judge it nor testify about it, or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says he is credible about his fellow’s. Learn from this that according to Rabbi Meir he would not permit [it], even though he was a ḥaver.

messages.text: But Rabbi Yehoshua said to me that yes, we did differentiate in this manner.

@Rabbi Tzadok Wait until the masters of the shields [ba’alei terisin], a reference to the Torah scholars who battle in the war of Torah, enter the study hall, at which point we will discuss this issue.

notes.he: מגינים. תלמידי חכמים הנלחמים במלחמה של תורה:
notes.en: Masters of the shields: shield-bearers; Torah scholars who fight in the war of Torah.

notes.he: חכמים:
notes.en: Masters of the shields: Sages.

messages.text: When the Torah scholars entered the study hall, the questioner stood before everyone present and asked: With regard to blemishes found on a firstborn animal, didn’t we differentiate between a priest who is a ḥaver and a priest who is an ignoramus?

notes.he: בפ' נערה בנדרים בירושלמי דריש מדכתיב ועמדו שני האנשים בוי"ו דשואל הלכות ואגדות צריך לעמוד:
notes.en: The questioner stood and asked: In the chapter Na’ara [HaMeorasa] of Nedarim, the Jerusalem Talmud derives from “And the two men shall stand,” [written] with the vav, that one who asks about halakhot and aggadot must stand.

notes.he: ר' צדוק:
notes.en: The questioner stood: Rabbi Tzadok.

messages.text: No, we did not.

notes.he: דלא רצה להורות הלכה לפני ר"ג:
notes.en: Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: No: because he did not want to issue a halakhic ruling in the presence of Rabban Gamliel.

messages.text: @Rabbi Yehoshua But they said to me in your name that yes, we did differentiate.
Yehoshua, stand on your feet and they will testify against you that you did, in fact, say that we differentiated in such a case.

notes.he: לא גרסי' ויעידו בך לא כאן ולא בפרק תפלת השחר ברישיה (ברכות כז:) דמה עדות שייך כאן אלא בסנהדרין בריש פרק כהן גדול (סנהדרין דף יט.) גרסינן ליה גבי עובדא דינאי ואגב פשטא דהתם נכתב כאן:
notes.en: Stand on your feet and they will testify against you: We do not read “and they will testify against you”, neither here nor at the beginning of the chapter Tefillat HaShaḥar (Berakhot 27b), for what testimony is relevant here? Rather, it is read in Sanhedrin, at the beginning of the chapter Kohen Gadol (Sanhedrin 19a), in the incident of Yannai, and from familiarity with the wording there it was written here.

messages.text: How should I act in this situation? If I were alive and Rabbi Tzadok were dead, the living can contradict the dead, and I could deny issuing that ruling. Now that I am alive and he is alive, how can the living contradict the living? I have no choice but to admit that I said it.
messages.lead: Rabbi Yehoshua stood on his feet and said:

notes.he: יכול להכחישו:
notes.en: How shall I act: [i.e., how] can I contradict him?

notes.he: הייתי יכול להכחיש ולומר לא אמרתי:
notes.en: If I were alive and he were dead: I could contradict him and say, “I did not say it.”

notes.dh: היאך יכול החי להכחיש את החי
notes.he: ודאי כך אמרתי וחוזרני בי:
notes.en: How can the living contradict the living: certainly I said so, and I retract.

notes.he: כלומר סבור הייתי להעלים ואיני יכול ובקונט' פירש דודאי כך אמרתי וחזרתי בי וא"א כן דבפרק תפלת השחר (ברכות דף כז:) פסק שם הלכה כמותו:
notes.en: How can the living contradict the living: That is, I thought to conceal it, but I cannot. And the Kuntres [Rashi] explained: certainly I said so, and I retract. But it cannot be so, for in the chapter Tefillat HaShaḥar (Berakhot 27b) the halakha is ruled there in accordance with him [Rabbi Yehoshua].

messages.text: In the meantime, Rabban Gamliel was standing and lecturing, and Rabbi Yehoshua all the while was standing on his feet, as Rabban Gamliel did not instruct him to sit. He remained standing in deference to the Nasi.

notes.he: והיינו דאמר בברכות (אתא) בבכורות צעריה:
notes.en: And this is what it says in Berakhot: “He distressed him [also] in [the matter of] firstborns.”

messages.text: This continued for some time, until it aroused great resentment against Rabban Gamliel, and all of the people assembled began murmuring and said to Ḥutzpit the disseminator: Stop conveying Rabban Gamliel’s lecture, and he stopped.

notes.he: שתוק ושתק:
notes.en: Stop, and he stopped: be silent, and he was silent.

notes.he: מעשרה הרוגי מלכות:
notes.en: Rabbi Ḥutzpit the disseminator: one of the ten martyrs executed by the [Roman] government.

notes.he: שתוק:
notes.en: Stop: be silent.

messages.text: Mishna
A priest is deemed credible to say: I showed this firstborn animal to an expert and he ruled that it is blemished.

notes.he: לחכם ואמר לי שמום קבוע הוא ושוחטו ובלבד שיהו לו עדים שלא הטילו בו:
notes.en: Mishna. I showed this firstborn: to a Sage, and he told me that it is a permanent blemish; and he may slaughter it, provided he has witnesses that he did not inflict it on it.

messages.text: Gemara
A priest is deemed credible to say: An Israelite gave me this firstborn animal with its blemish already inflicted upon it.

notes.he: לחכם בכור זה נתן [לי] ישראל במום זה שבו:
notes.en: Gemara. A priest is deemed credible to say: to a Sage, “An Israelite gave [me] this firstborn with this blemish that is on it.”

messages.text: What is the reason? With regard to any matter that is likely to be revealed, people do not lie about it. Since the Israelite can be questioned with regard to the veracity of the priest’s claim, it is assumed that the priest will not risk lying.

notes.he: דאתי חכם ואמר לא התרתיו לך:
notes.en: That is likely to be revealed: for the Sage may come and say, “I did not permit it to you.”

notes.he: דמצי למישייליה לחכם אם התירו לו אם לא:
notes.en: That is likely to be revealed: for one can ask the Sage whether he permitted it to him or not.

messages.text: We learn a similar principle in the mishna as well: A priest is deemed credible to say: I showed this firstborn animal to an expert and he ruled that it is blemished. What is the reason the priest’s claim is deemed credible? Is it not because we say that with regard to any matter that is likely to be revealed, people do not lie about it?
messages.quote: A priest is deemed credible to say: I showed this firstborn

messages.text: Perhaps there, in the case of the mishna, the reason the priest’s claim is accepted is that he would not eat sacrificial meat outside the Temple courtyard. If an expert had not permitted the meat, the priest would not eat it.
messages.quote: Is it not because we say

notes.he: לא לעולם אימא לך מילתא דעבידא לאיגלויי משקרי אינשי והכא היינו טעמא דמהימן דלא חשידי כהני לאכול קדשים תמימים בחוץ הלכך אי לאו דשרי ליה חכם לא הוה אמר שרא ליה ושחיט ליה בלא התרת מומחה:
notes.en: No; actually I can tell you that about a matter likely to be revealed people do lie. And here, this is the reason he is credible: priests are not suspected of eating unblemished consecrated animals outside [the Temple]. Therefore, if the Sage had not permitted it to him, he would not say “he permitted it to me” and slaughter it without an expert’s permission.

notes.he: דכיון דשחט הוא ואמר הראיתיו לחכם הוא ובעל מום הוא דמהימן דכיון דקאכיל ליה מידע ידע דקדשים בחוץ לא מצי אכיל ובודאי הראהו:
notes.en: It is there: since he slaughtered it and says, “I showed it to a Sage and it is blemished,” he is credible. For since he is eating it, he surely knows that he may not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple], and he certainly showed it.

messages.text: But here, in Rav’s case, where the priest claims an Israelite gave him an already blemished animal, since priests are suspected of causing blemishes and claiming that it was inadvertent, they are also suspected of causing a blemish and claiming it was given to them in that state by an Israelite.

notes.he: דקא מחוי ליה לחכם ואמר במום [זה] נתן לי ישראל כדי שלא יצטרך להביא עדים שמאליו נפל בו כיון דחשידי כהני להטיל מום ולמימר נפל מאליו חשידי נמי להטיל מום ולמימר ישראל נתנו לי במומו:
notes.en: But here: where he shows it to the Sage and says, “An Israelite gave it to me with [this] blemish,” so that he will not need to bring witnesses that it fell on it by itself. Since priests are suspected of inflicting a blemish and saying it fell by itself, they are also suspected of inflicting a blemish and saying, “An Israelite gave it to me with its blemish.”

notes.he: בכהן שאמר בכור זה נתן לי ישראל במומו כיון דחי הוא דלא שחטיה לא מהימן ולא שרינן למישחטיה דחשידי דילמא איהו שדא ביה מומא וליתא לדרב יהודה דעבידא לאיגלויי דמצי למישייליה אי זבין ליה:
notes.en: But here: with a priest who said, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” since it is alive and he has not slaughtered it, he is not credible, and we do not permit him to slaughter it, for they are suspected; perhaps he inflicted a blemish on it. And Rav Yehuda’s [reason], that it is likely to be revealed because one can ask [the Israelite] whether he sold it to him, does not hold.

messages.text: Rav Sheizevi raises an objection to Rav’s ruling from a mishna:

In the case of one who says to someone who is not trusted with regard to tithe: Purchase produce for me from someone who is trusted with regard to tithes, i.e., one who does not purchase produce from an ignoramus, who generally does not separate tithes; or if he says: Purchase produce for me from someone who tithes, i.e., even from one who purchases produce from an ignoramus but is careful to set aside tithes upon purchasing the produce, the agent is not deemed credible to claim that he fulfilled the condition of the one who appointed him.

notes.he: שאינו לוקח פירות מעם הארץ או ממי שלוקח מעם הארץ ומעשר דמאי קודם שימכרם:
notes.en: Buy for me from one who is trusted: who does not buy produce from an ignoramus; or from one who buys from an ignoramus and tithes the demai before selling it.

notes.he: שליח זה נאמן לומר שמנאמן לקחתיו:
notes.en: Is not [credible]: this agent is [not] credible to say, “I bought it from a trusted person.”

messages.text: According to Rav, why isn’t the agent deemed credible? Say the principle that with regard to any matter that is likely to be revealed, people do not lie about it.
It is different there,
messages.quote: why isn’t the agent deemed credible?

messages.text: as he has the easy option of extricating himself from the accusation that he did not fulfill the condition of the one who appointed him, by claiming that in his opinion the individual from whom he purchased the produce was to be trusted. Since the issue of the third party’s trustworthiness is subjective, the agent is not afraid to lie.

notes.he: ולמימר אי לדידך לא מהימן אנא הוה חשיבנא ליה מהימן הלכך לא מירתת מעיקרא:
notes.en: As he has [a way] of extricating himself: by saying, “If to you he is not trustworthy, I considered him trustworthy.” Therefore he is not afraid from the outset.

notes.he: שאני התם דמצי לאישתמוטי שליח דמצי ואמר לאו מהאי זבניה אלא מאחרינא אפילו מעם הארץ דמצי אמר אפילו עם הארץ נאמן הוא עלי ליקח ממנו. הלכך אינו נאמן השליח:
notes.en: It is different there, as the agent can extricate himself: for he can say, “I did not buy it from this one but from another, even from an ignoramus,” since he can say, “Even an ignoramus is trustworthy to me to buy from him.” Therefore the agent is not credible.

messages.text: The latter clause of this mishna certainly supports the ruling of Rav, that people do not lie with regard to any matter that will be revealed. How so?
messages.quote: Purchase produce for me from someone who is trusted

messages.text: The latter clause states that if the one instructed the agent to purchase produce specifically from so-and-so, who is reliable with regard to tithes, then this agent is deemed credible to claim that he adhered to the instructions. Since the one who appointed him mentioned a specific individual, the agent is not suspected of lying, as that individual can be subsequently questioned.

notes.he: דהזכיר לו משלח שם הנאמן הרי זה נאמן השליח דחייש שמא יתבעני ונמצאתי משקר. והך סיפא ודאי מסייעא ליה לרב יהודה דמילתא דעבידא לאיגלויי לא משקרי בה אינשי:
notes.en: From so-and-so: since the sender mentioned to him the name of the trusted person, this agent is credible, for he worries, “Perhaps he will question me and I will be found lying.” And this latter clause certainly supports Rav Yehuda, that people do not lie about a matter that is likely to be revealed.

notes.he: היכא דאמר ליה קח לי מאיש פלוני נאמן הרי זה נאמן השליח לומר שלקח ממנו דהשתא לא מצי לאשתמוטי:
notes.en: The latter clause supports Rav Yehuda. Where he said to him, “Buy for me from so-and-so, who is trusted,” this agent is credible to say that he bought from him, for now he cannot extricate himself.

messages.text: There, in the mishna, since the agent has a claimant, he is afraid to lie. In other words, since the one who appointed him specified an individual, the agent presumes that he intends to verify the matter, and therefore he will not risk lying.

notes.he: כלומר מהא לא תסייעיה דהתם מירתת שליח כיון דחזי דקפיד משלח להזכיר שם האיש סבר ודאי יתבענו אבל גבי בכור לא מירתת האי כהן דסבר מי יטרח לחפש אחר דברי ולישאל לאותו ישראל אם נתנו לי במומו:
notes.en: There, since there is a claimant, he is afraid: that is, do not support him from this. For there the agent is afraid: since he sees that the sender took care to mention the man’s name, he thinks he will certainly question him. But with the firstborn, this priest is not afraid, for he thinks: who will bother to look into my words and ask that Israelite whether he gave it to me with its blemish?

notes.he: מהא לא מסייעי ליה התם מאיש פלוני נאמן (אמאי) [ודאי] השליח דכיון דאית ליה תובע דמשלח קא משייל לאותו פלוני נאמן אי זבן שלוחיה מיניה מירתת השליח ולא זבין אלא מההוא:
notes.en: But it is not so: there is no support for him from this. There, [regarding] “from so-and-so, who is trusted,” the agent is [certainly credible], for since he has a claimant, as the sender will ask that trusted so-and-so whether his agent bought from him, the agent is afraid and buys only from that one.

messages.text: By contrast, in Rav’s case, since it was the priest who volunteered the information that a specific Israelite gave him an already blemished firstborn animal, he is not concerned that the examiner might seek out the Israelite to confirm the actual facts.

notes.he: אבל כהן שאמר בכור זה נתן לי ישראל במומו לית ליה תובע ליכא דחייש למישיילי לישראל אי יהבי ניהליה במומיה להכי לא מסייעא ליה:
notes.en: But a priest who said, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” has no claimant: no one bothers to ask the Israelite whether he gave it to him with its blemish. Therefore it does not support him.

messages.text: From where does Yehuda know this halakha? Actually, I taught this halakha to Giddul in Rav’s name and Giddul, in turn, taught it to Rav Yehuda.
messages.quote: A priest is deemed credible to say: An Israelite gave me this firstborn

notes.he: דאמרן לעיל נאמן כהן לומר בכור זה נתן לי ישראל במומו:
notes.en: From where does Yehuda [know] this: what we said above: a priest is credible to say, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish.”

notes.he: אני שניתיה לגידול והוא שנאה לרב יהודה והכי אמרי לגידול נאמן ישראל לומר כו'. ל"א בגידול קבעתה לחכם א' גדול שניתיה:
notes.en: I fixed it with Giddul: I taught it to Giddul, and he taught it to Rav Yehuda; and this is what I said to Giddul: an Israelite is credible to say, etc. Another version: “I fixed it with a great one [gadol]”: I taught it to one great Sage.

notes.he: כלומר אני למדתיה לגידול וגידול למדה לרב יהודה:
notes.en: This: I fixed it with Giddul. That is, I taught it to Giddul, and Giddul taught it to Rav Yehuda.

messages.text: But Giddul corrupted my statement, as this is how I said it to him: An Israelite is deemed credible to say: I gave this firstborn animal to a priest with its blemish already inflicted upon it, and it may be slaughtered and eaten.
An Israelite? It is obvious that he is deemed credible to issue this claim, as he has no use for the firstborn animal.
messages.quote: An Israelite is deemed credible to say

notes.he: דהא לא חשידי אמומי:
notes.en: An Israelite? That is obvious: for they are not suspected about blemishes.

messages.text: No, this ruling is necessary, as it is referring to an animal that was young when the Israelite gave it to the priest and it grew older by the time of his testimony. This ruling is necessary, lest you say that as the animal grew older in the interim, perhaps the Israelite does not recognize it and mistakenly assumes that it was the animal he gave the priest, when in fact it is a different firstborn animal upon which the priest intentionally caused a blemish. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba therefore teaches us that the Israelite is trusted to recognize the animal he gave the priest.

notes.he: שהיה קטן הטלה כשנתנו לו:
notes.en: With a young one: the lamb was small when he gave it to him.

notes.dh: מהו דתימא לא קים ליה בגויה
notes.he: דמשום דהגדיל הטלה אינו מכירו ושמא אחר הוא והאי כהן הטיל בו מום:
notes.en: Lest you say he is not sure of it: because the lamb has grown, he does not recognize it, and perhaps it is another one, and this priest inflicted a blemish on it.

notes.he: כלומר קטן היה אותו ישראל כשנתן לו זה הבכור לכהן במומו ועכשיו כשהו' גדול מעיד עליו דהוא המום עצמו שהיה בו כשנתתיו לו:
notes.en: No, it is necessary in the case of a minor who grew up: that is, that Israelite was a minor when he gave this firstborn with its blemish to the priest, and now, when he is an adult, he testifies about it that it is the same blemish that was on it when he gave it to him. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “a young one” as the Israelite, not the animal; Rashi and the Davidson English read it as the animal.]

notes.he: מהו דתימא לא קים ליה ביה בהאי מום דהיינו הוא משום דקטן הוה ולא מדכר קמ"ל דנאמן:
notes.en: Lest you say he is not sure of it [a note in the printed text corrects the wording to “lo kim leih beih”]: whether this is the very blemish that was on it when he gave it to him, because he was a minor and does not remember. [Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba] teaches us that he is credible.

messages.text: In Sura, they teach the halakha in accordance with the latter version, as stated by Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba, that an Israelite is deemed credible to testify. In Pumbedita, they teach the halakha in accordance with the first version, as taught by Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, that even a priest is deemed credible if he claims that an Israelite gave him an already blemished firstborn animal.

notes.he: נאמן ישראל:
notes.en: In accordance with the latter version: an Israelite is credible.

notes.he: דאפי' הכהן נאמן. והלכתא אפי' כלישנא קמא:
notes.en: In accordance with the first version: that even the priest is credible. And the halakha is even in accordance with the first version.

messages.text: And the halakha is in accordance with even the first version.

notes.he: ואע"ג דהכא פסקינן דמילתא דעבידא לאגלויי לא משקר מ"מ לא הימניה לע"א אלא משום דדייקא ומנסבא א"נ דלמא כיון דרחמא לה לא דייקא ולמ"ד הכא אינו נאמן אפי' במילתא דעבידא לאיגלויי יש לחלק בין האי כהן לעד א"נ גבי אשה הקילו משום עיגונא ועוד דדייקא:
notes.en: And the halakha is even in accordance with the first version: And even though here we rule that people do not lie about a matter likely to be revealed, nevertheless [in the case of a woman whose husband is reported dead] one witness is believed only because she investigates carefully and [only then] marries. Alternatively, [both reasons are needed because] perhaps, since she loves him, she would not investigate carefully. And according to the one who says here that [the priest] is not credible even about a matter likely to be revealed, one can distinguish between this priest and a [single] witness. Alternatively, with regard to a woman they were lenient because of [her becoming] an aguna, and also because she investigates carefully.

notes.he: [לישנא אחרינא קטן הוה הכבש] והלכתא כלישנא קמא דכל מילתא דעבידא לאיגלויי לא משקרי:
notes.en: [Another version: the lamb was young.] And the halakha follows the first version, for about any matter likely to be revealed people do not lie.

messages.text: In this regard, Rafram, who resided in Pumbedita, had a firstborn animal and he gave it to a priest in an unblemished state. The priest went and caused a blemish in it.

One day, Rafram had an affliction in his eyes, which rendered it difficult for him to open them. The priest to whom Rafram had given the firstborn animal brought it before him, as an expert examiner, for him to deem the animal permitted.

notes.he: רפרם בעיניה:
notes.en: One day he was ill: Rafram, in his eyes.

notes.he: האי כהן לבוכרא קמיה למיחזי אם מום קבוע הוא וסבר ההוא כהן השתא חייש בעיניה ולא יכיר שזה הוא שנתן לי בלא מום:
notes.en: He brought it: this priest brought the firstborn before him to see whether it is a permanent blemish. And that priest thought: now his eyes hurt, and he will not recognize that this is the one he gave me without a blemish.

notes.he: חש רפרם בעייניה:
notes.en: One day: Rafram’s eyes hurt.

notes.he: ההוא בכור עצמו דיהב ליה דסבר השתא דחש בעייניה לא מבשקר ליה:
notes.en: He brought it before him: that very firstborn that he had given him, for he thought: now that his eyes hurt, he will not recognize it.

messages.text: An Israelite gave me this firstborn animal with its blemish upon it.
Rafram forced his eyes open and saw the animal and recognized it [bashkerei] as the one he himself had given the priest.

notes.he: פתח עינו בכח:
notes.en: He forced his eyes open: he opened his eye with force.

notes.he: שהכיר שהוא נתנו לו בלא מום:
notes.en: He saw it and recognized it [bashkerei]: he recognized that he had given it to him without a blemish.

notes.he: פי' ראהו והכיר בו דבשקריה הוא לשון הכרה כמו מאן דבעל עובדת כוכבים דמשכה ליה עורלתיה ולא מבשקר ליה בפ' עושין פסין (עירובין יט.) וכמו חלף קמייהו ולא בשקריה בפרק בתרא דיבמות (דף קכ.) ובקונטרס לא פירש כן:
notes.en: He saw it and recognized it [bashkerei]: This means he saw it and recognized it, for bashkerei is an expression of recognition, as in “one who has relations with a gentile woman, his foreskin is drawn and [Abraham] does not recognize him [mivashker leih]” in the chapter Osin Pasin (Eruvin 19a), and as in “he passed before them and they did not recognize him [bashkerei]” in the last chapter of Yevamot (120a). And the Kuntres [Rashi] did not explain it so.

notes.he: כלומר פקח רפרם לעיניו ביותר:
notes.en: He forced his eyes open: that is, Rafram opened his eyes wide.

messages.text: Is it not I who gave this firstborn animal to you?
And even so, Rafram was unconcerned by the matter of the priest’s attempted chicanery, as he maintained that it is only this priest who is impudent, but all other priests are not impudent.

notes.he: רפרם למילתא למימר דלא יהיה עוד כהן נאמן לומר בכור זה נתנו לי ישראל במומו:
notes.en: He was unconcerned: Rafram, about the matter, [that is, he did not] say that a priest should no longer be credible to say, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish.”

notes.he: שהרי הוא החזיק עצמו כחצוף לשני דברים אחד שהטיל בו מום ועוד דהיה לו להראותו לחכם אחר והראהו לזה עצמו שנתנו לו:
notes.en: It is this one who is impudent: for he showed himself impudent in two respects: first, that he inflicted a blemish on it; and further, that he should have shown it to another Sage, and he showed it to the very one who gave it to him.

notes.he: למיגזר דלא ליהמנוה לשום כהן דאמר בכור זה נתן לי ישראל במומו אלא נאמן. דסבר האי הוא דחציף דעבד הכי:
notes.en: And even so he was unconcerned by the matter: [that is, he did not] decree that no priest who says, “An Israelite gave me this firstborn with its blemish,” should be believed; rather, he is credible. For he held: it is this one who is impudent, who did this.

messages.text: This scenario did not cause Rafram to discredit any other priest’s claim that he received a blemished firstborn animal from an Israelite, as this was an exceptional case. This priest demonstrated extreme impudence by bringing it to be examined by Rafram himself, and therefore one cannot draw conclusions about the behavior of other priests from this incident.

There was a certain firstborn animal, one of whose eyes was larger than the other, whose owner came before Rav Ashi to have it deemed fit for slaughter on account of its blemish. Rav Ashi was uncertain as to who brought the animal for examination.

notes.he: עינו אחת גדולה ואחת קטנה:
notes.en: Sarua: one of its eyes large and one small.

messages.text: For what should we be concerned with regard to this animal? In a case of such a blemish, whether it is a priest who brought it for examination, or whether it is an Israelite, there is no concern that the blemish might have been intentionally caused, as this is clearly a firstborn animal whose blemish was already with it naturally.

notes.he: שלא היה מכיר בזה אם כהן אם ישראל ואמר ואפילו הוא כהן וחשוד על הבכור אין כאן חשדא שהרי כך נולד:
notes.en: Whether it is a priest, whether it is an Israelite: for he did not know whether this was a priest or an Israelite, and he said: even if he is a priest and suspected about the firstborn, there is no suspicion here, for it was born this way.

notes.he: מאי ניחוש ליה האי מום ודאי בידי שמים הוא אי כהן הוא אי ישראל הוא דאתייה הרי ודאי מומו עמו ומותר:
notes.en: What should we be concerned about? This blemish is certainly by the hand of Heaven. Whether it is a priest or an Israelite who brought it, certainly its blemish is with it, and it is permitted.

messages.text: @Rav Ashi But perhaps it is an Israelite who brought the firstborn animal, and Rav Yehuda says that one may not examine the firstborn animal of an Israelite unless a priest is present with him in order to receive the animal if it is established as fit for slaughter.

notes.he: דשמא אם יאמר לו קבוע ישחטנו ויאכל הוא דכיון דקבוע הוא הרי הוא נאכל לכל אדם אלא שגזילת כהן הוא והאי לא חייש לגזילה ואכיל ליה:
notes.en: Unless a priest is with him: for perhaps, if [the expert] tells him it is permanent, he will slaughter it and eat it [himself]. For since it is permanent it may be eaten by anyone, except that it is the stolen property of a priest, and this one is not concerned about theft and eats it.

notes.he: דאתי ואין רואין בכור לישראל אא"כ כהן עמו דמחשדינן ליה שמא בתר דקא שרינן ליה לא יהיב ליה לכהן אלא הוא גופיה אכיל ליה להכי בעינן כהן עמו דלאלתר ליהביה ניהליה ואמאי קא שרית ליה אי דישראל הוא:
notes.en: But perhaps it is an Israelite who came, and one does not examine a firstborn for an Israelite unless a priest is with him, for we suspect that perhaps, after we permit it to him, he will not give it to the priest but will eat it himself. Therefore we require a priest with him, so that he will give it to him immediately. So why do you permit it, if it is an Israelite’s?

messages.text: Rav Yehuda is concerned that if the Israelite’s firstborn animal is deemed fit for slaughter when no priest is present, the Israelite might improperly use the animal for his own purposes. If so, how can you, Rav Ashi, say that there is no problem if this animal was brought by an Israelite?

@Ravina How can these cases be compared? There, where the presence of a priest is required, it is referring to a case where the halakhic status of the blemish has yet to be determined. Now, granted an Israelite will not risk eating sacrificial meat outside the Temple courtyard, as that incurs a penalty of karet, and he therefore would have the blemish’s status determined by an expert.

notes.he: גבי שאר מומין שאין מובהקין איכא למיחשדיה לישראל שמא יגזול את הכהן ואע"ג דאדם כשר הוא בהא מילתא דלא בעי לשוחטו אלא ע"פ מומחה דנהי דקדשים בחוץ לא אכיל דבכרת הוא השוחט קדשים בחוץ מיהו אגזילה דכהן דלאו בעלמא חשיד:
notes.en: How can these be compared? There: with other blemishes, which are not clear-cut, there is reason to suspect the Israelite that he may rob the priest. And even though he is a proper person in this matter, in that he wants to slaughter it only on the basis of an expert, granted that he will not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple], for one who slaughters consecrated animals outside is [liable to] karet; nevertheless, about robbing a priest, which is a mere prohibition, he is suspected.

notes.he: בספק מום משום הכי אין רואין אלא א"כ כהן עמו נהי דבבכור תם קא מחמיר ישראל דקדשים בחוץ לא אכיל אבל אממוניה דכהן אבעל מום דלית ליה קדושה חשיד למיכליה להכי אין רואין אא"כ כהן עמו אבל הכא בהאי שרוע מכדי מידע ידע ישראל דמום מובהק הוא וכיון דלא עבר על כבודו של חכם בודאי איסורא לא עביד דניחוש להכי:
notes.en: How can these be compared? There, with a doubtful blemish, one does not examine it unless a priest is with him for this reason: granted that with an unblemished firstborn the Israelite is strict, for he will not eat consecrated meat outside [the Temple], but regarding the priest’s property, a blemished animal that has no sanctity, he is suspected of eating it. That is why one does not examine unless a priest is with him. But here, with this sarua, the Israelite surely knows that it is a clear-cut blemish, and since he did not neglect the honor of the Sage, he certainly will not commit a transgression, that we should suspect him of it.

messages.text: But he is suspected with regard to the property of a priest. Although the Israelite will have the status of the animal confirmed before risking a prohibition that entails karet, he might steal the firstborn offering if it is established as fit for consumption.

Conversely, here, in the case of the animal that had one eye larger than the other, since even an Israelite knows that this is a clear-cut blemish and the animal is clearly fit for slaughter, what is the reason he brought the animal before the Sages for examination? He brought it out of respect for the Sage.

notes.he:
כדאמר לקמן ג' מתירין את הבכור במקום שאין מומחה ובמקום שיש מומחה לא:
פסק אבל הא פשיטא דבלא התרה אינו נשחט אפילו יש בו מום מובהק אלא ע"פ ג' או מומחה:
notes.en: Out of respect for the Sage: as it says below, three may permit a firstborn where there is no expert, and where there is an expert, not. Ruling: but this is obvious, that without permission it may not be slaughtered even if it has a clear-cut blemish, except on the basis of three or of an expert.

messages.text: Now, if this Israelite does not neglect the respect due a Sage, would he commit a transgression and steal the possession of the priest? Certainly not. Therefore, in our case an Israelite would be trustworthy, and the presence of a priest is unnecessary.

notes.he: בתמיה. ודאי לא יגזול:
notes.en: He would commit a transgression? Said in astonishment: certainly he will not rob.

notes.dh: על כבודו דחכם לא עבר איסורא עבד
notes.he: וא"ת מהאי טעמא לישתרו בלא עדות כל בכורות שהכהנים מביאין לפנינו שיש בהם מום מובהק וי"ל דשאני כהן שירא לאוכלו בלא התרת חכם פן יתגלה הדבר מתוך כך שהטיל בו מום אבל האי ישראל אין לומר שמביא לפני חכם פן יודע שרוצה לאוכלו ולגוזלו לכהן שהרי גם עתה בשביל כך לא יתברר שלא יאכלנו הוא עצמו:
notes.en: He does not neglect the respect due a Sage; would he commit a transgression: And if you say: for this reason, all firstborns with a clear-cut blemish that priests bring before us should be permitted without testimony! One can say: a priest is different, for he is afraid to eat it without a Sage’s permission, lest through this the matter be revealed that he inflicted a blemish on it. But of this Israelite one cannot say that he brings it before a Sage lest it become known that he wants to eat it and rob the priest of it, for even now, by doing this, it will not be made clear that he will not eat it himself.

messages.text: Mishna
Everyone is deemed credible to testify about the blemishes of an animal tithe offering, even the owner who is the beneficiary of a ruling that it is blemished.

notes.dh: מתני' הכל נאמנין על מומי מעשר
notes.he: להעיד שמאליו נפל בו. ובספק מעשר קאמר כגון קרא לתשיעי עשירי דאמרי' בפ' אחרון (לקמן בכורות נט.) אינו נאכל ואין לו תקנה אלא במום:
notes.en: Mishna. Everyone is credible about the blemishes of a tithe: to testify that it fell on it by itself. And it is speaking of a doubtful tithe, for example where he called the ninth “tenth”, about which we say in the last chapter (below, Bekhorot 59a) that it is not eaten and has no remedy except through a blemish.

messages.text: Gemara

What is the reason that even the owner is deemed credible to testify? The reason is that had he wanted, he could have caused a blemish in it initially, in a permitted manner, before tithing his animals.

But when he leads his animals out of the gate in order to tithe them, does he know which of them will emerge as the tenth, that you say he could have initially blemished that specific animal before it assumed the tithe status?

notes.he: בפתח עשירי שיטיל בו מום מעיקרא:
notes.en: Gemara. Does he know which will emerge: at the opening, as tenth, that he could inflict a blemish on it from the outset?

messages.text: And if you would say that he intentionally leads an animal out as the head of the ten, i.e., so that it is the last of ten to emerge, one may not do so, as the Merciful One states: “He shall not search whether it be good or bad”, which teaches that the animal tithe may not be led out intentionally but must exit of its own accord.

verse.he: לֹא יְבַקֵּר בֵּין־טוֹב לָרַע וְלֹא יְמִירֶנּוּ וְאִם־הָמֵר יְמִירֶנּוּ וְהָיָה־הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ יִהְיֶה־קֹּדֶשׁ לֹא יִגָּאֵל׃
verse.en: One must not look out for good as against bad, or make substitution for it. If one does make substitution for it, then it and its substitute shall both be holy: it cannot be redeemed.

notes.he: כלומר בעשירי:
notes.en: At the head of ten: that is, as the tenth.

messages.text: Rather, this is the meaning of the Gemara’s initial answer: The reason is that had he wanted, he could have caused a blemish in his entire flock, in a permitted manner, before leading them through the gate in order to tithe them.
Mishna

With regard to a firstborn animal whose eye was blinded or whose foreleg was severed or whose hind leg was broken, all of which obviously render the animal permanently blemished, that animal may be slaughtered on the basis of the ruling of three regular Jews who attend the synagogue, and it does not require a ruling by one of the Sages.

notes.he: דהוי מום מובהק:
notes.en: Mishna. Whose eye was blinded: which is a clear-cut blemish.

notes.he: שאינן חכמים:
notes.en: Synagogue-goers: who are not Sages.

messages.text: Even if there is a court of twenty-three Sages there, it may be slaughtered only on the basis of the ruling of an expert in judging blemishes.
Gemara

The permitting of the slaughter of a firstborn animal outside of Eretz Yisrael, where a firstborn offering is unfit for sacrifice even when the Temple is standing, may be performed on the basis of the ruling of three regular Jews who attend the synagogue.
messages.lead: Rabbi Simlai and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia both say in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and some say that Rabbi Simlai and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi both say in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia:

notes.he: שאינו ראוי להקריב ואפילו בזמן בית המקדש במס' תמורה (דף כא:):
notes.en: Gemara. Outside the Land: where it is not fit to be sacrificed, even in the time of the Temple, [as stated] in tractate Temura (21b).

notes.dh: התרת בכור בחוצה לארץ על פי שלשה בני הכנסת
notes.he: ממתניתין לא שמעינן ליה דאיכא לאוקמה בזמן הזה אבל בזמן שבית המקדש קיים ה"ל למיגזר חוצה לארץ אטו ארץ ישראל שלא להקל להתיר על פי שלשה בני הכנסת ועוד משום דאיכא למאן דאמר בתמורה פרק אלו קדשים (תמורה דף כא.) דבכורות חוצה לארץ אם באו תמימים יקרבו:
notes.en: The permitting of a firstborn outside the Land on the basis of three synagogue-goers: We would not learn this from our mishna, for it can be explained as referring to nowadays; but when the Temple stands one might have decreed [regarding] outside the Land on account of the Land of Israel, not to be lenient and permit [it] on the basis of three synagogue-goers. And further, because there is an opinion in Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (Temura 21a), that firstborns from outside the Land, if they arrived unblemished, are sacrificed.

messages.text: And this ruling applies specifically in a case of clear-cut blemishes, i.e., those blemishes which clearly permit the slaughter of the firstborn animal.
messages.quote: on the basis of the ruling of three regular Jews who attend the synagogue

messages.text: What is Rava teaching us by this statement? We already learn this in the mishna: With regard to a firstborn animal whose eye was blinded or whose foreleg was severed or whose hind leg was broken, that animal may be slaughtered on the basis of the ruling of three regular Jews who attend the synagogue.

notes.he: מאי קמ"ל תנינא בכור כו' ומתני' בחוצה לארץ ובזמן הזה עסקינן מדקתני זקן ושערו מדולדל דאי ס"ד בזמן ביהמ"ק ליקרבוה שריה:
notes.en: What is he teaching us? We learn: a firstborn, etc. And the mishna is dealing with outside the Land and nowadays, since it teaches [elsewhere] “old, with its hair hanging down”; for if it entered your mind [that it speaks of] the time of the Temple, they should have sacrificed it [before it grew old].

messages.text: The mishna is referring to clear-cut blemishes in contemporary times, in the absence of the Temple, when a firstborn animal is unfit to be brought as an offering. What, then, is the novelty of Rava’s statement?

notes.he: שלשה בני כנסת דלא בעינן מומחין גמורין:
notes.en: Three synagogue-goers: for we do not require full experts.

messages.text: If the halakha that three regular Jews may permit the slaughter of a firstborn animal is learned from the mishna alone, I would say that according to the mishna, the power invested in three regular Jews to permit the slaughter of a firstborn animal in the absence of the Temple nowadays, or outside of Eretz Yisrael during Temple times, applies even to a firstborn animal that has blemishes that are not clear-cut.

notes.he: ובמומין מובהקין הניכרים כגון נסמת עינו נקטעה:
notes.en: And with clear-cut blemishes, which are recognizable, such as an eye blinded or [a leg] severed.

messages.text: And the reason that the mishna specifically teaches a case of clear-cut blemishes is to convey the far-reaching nature of the opinion of Rabbi Yosei, who requires the examination of an expert even in such a case. Rava therefore teaches us that this is not so; rather, the mishna’s ruling is referring specifically to a case of clear-cut blemishes.

notes.he: דאפי' במובהקין קאמר דאינו נשחט אלא ע"פ מומחה:
notes.en: To convey the strength of Rabbi Yosei: that even with clear-cut [blemishes] he says that it may be slaughtered only on the basis of an expert.

messages.text: Three regular Jews may permit a firstborn animal with clear-cut blemishes in a place where there is no expert.
messages.lead: He was uncertain whether Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said it in the name of Rav and uncertain whether he said it in the name of Shmuel:

notes.he: אמרה לי ר' ירמיה משמיה דרב ספק אמרה לי משמיה דשמואל:
notes.en: Uncertain: uncertain whether he said it to me in the name of Rav, uncertain whether he said it to me in the name of Shmuel.

notes.he: במומין מובהקין:
notes.en: Three may permit the firstborn, etc.: with clear-cut blemishes.

messages.text: What is Rav Yehuda teaching us by this statement? We already learn this in the mishna: That animal may be slaughtered on the basis of the ruling of three regular Jews who attend the synagogue.
messages.quote: in a place where there is no expert

notes.he: הא דלא משני הכא לאפוקי מדרבי יוסי אע"ג דנימוקו עמו כדאמר בסמוך משום דא"כ הוה ליה לרב יהודה למימר הלכה כרבנן או אין הלכה כר' יוסי אבל ר' חייא דבסמוך נקט שני דברים מענין אחד התרת בכור והתרת נדרים:
notes.en: We learn: that animal may be slaughtered, etc.: Why does it not answer here that [Rav Yehuda’s ruling comes] to exclude the view of Rabbi Yosei, as is said shortly [of Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram], even though [Rabbi Yosei’s] reasoning is with him? Because if so, Rav Yehuda should have said “the halakha follows the Rabbis” or “the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosei.” But Rabbi Ḥiyya [Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram] below mentioned two matters on one subject, permitting a firstborn and permitting vows.

messages.text: If the halakha is learned from the mishna alone, I would say that three laymen may permit a firstborn animal with clear-cut blemishes even in a place where there is an expert. Rav Yehuda therefore teaches us that in a place where there is no expert, yes, three laymen may permit it. But in a place where there is an expert, three laymen are not invested with this power.

notes.he:
לאו דוקא מומחה שהמחוהו ב"ד דהא על רב אשי דלעיל אמרי' דאתיוה לקמיה ההוא שרוע משום כבודו דחכם וכל מופלג בחכמה ומומחה ראוי להתיר בכור ונדר ביחידי כדמשמע מדרב אשי דלעיל ובפ"ק דנדרים (דף ח:) גבי רבינא דהוה ליה נדרא לדביתהו ואתא לקמיה דרב אשי וכו' וקאמר ש"מ תלת כו' ויחיד מומחה שרי שמתא משמע קצת דיחיד מומחה הוי כרב אשי וכן ההיא דבפ"ק דסנהדרין (דף ה:) אא"כ היה מומחה לרבים דן אפי' יחידי לאו דוקא מומחה הנסמך כו' כדאמר ר"נ התם כגון אנא דן דיני ממונות:
פסק ומיהו בזמן הזה אין נראה שיהא שום אדם חשיב מומחה להתיר בכור ונדר ביחידי ולדון דיני ממונות:
notes.en: Where there is an expert, not: Not specifically an expert whom the court has authorized. For of Rav Ashi above we said that they brought that sarua before him out of respect for the Sage; and anyone outstanding in wisdom and expert is fit to permit a firstborn or a vow alone, as is implied by [the incident of] Rav Ashi above. And in the first chapter of Nedarim (8b), regarding Ravina, who had a vow concerning his wife and came before Rav Ashi, etc., it says “learn from it three [things]”, etc., “and a single expert may release a ban”; this implies somewhat that a single expert is [someone] like Rav Ashi. And similarly that [statement] in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (5b), “but if he was an expert for the public, he may judge even alone,” does not mean specifically an ordained expert, etc., as Rav Naḥman said there: “For example, one like me may judge monetary cases [alone].” Ruling: However, nowadays it does not appear that any person is considered an expert to permit a firstborn or a vow alone, or to judge monetary cases [alone].

messages.text: A group of three laymen may permit a blemished firstborn animal in a place where there is no expert to consult, and likewise a group of three laymen may dissolve a vow in a place where there is no Sage.

notes.dh: שלשה מתירין את הנדר במקום שאין חכם
notes.he: בענין זה דפ"ק דנדרים (ח:) [דאמרי'] לא שרי ליה לאיניש למישרי נדרא באתרא דרביה ומיהו ההיא אפי' יש שם מומחה אחר אין לאותו מומחה להתיר במקום רבו כמו רבינא במקום רב אשי:
notes.en: Three may dissolve a vow where there is no Sage: Compare in this matter the first chapter of Nedarim (8b), [where we say] a person may not dissolve a vow in the place of his teacher. However, there, even if another expert is present, that expert may not dissolve [it] in the place of his teacher, like Ravina in the place of Rav Ashi.
